title: Soil and Geological Science
description: Deep dive into Jurassic geology and the differences between Kimmeridgian and Portlandian soils

lessons.0.slides.0.description: Understanding the geological history behind Burgundy's soil formation
lessons.0.slides.1.title: An Ocean 200 Million Years Ago
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy's soils were formed primarily during the Jurassic Period (200–145 million years ago). The land was then a warm, shallow sea where the remains of marine organisms — corals, shellfish, plankton — accumulated layer upon layer. Over millions of years of compression and chemical change, they became the limestone, marl, and clay we see today. The microscopic differences in these ancient rocks are what create today's differences in wine style.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🌍 Burgundy During the Jurassic
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Early Jurassic (200–175 million years ago): deep-sea environment, dark shale, anoxic sediment
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Middle Jurassic (175–160 million years ago): shallow-sea environment, iron-rich, forming red-brown clay
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Late Jurassic (160–145 million years ago): most important period, forming the Kimmeridgian layer
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: Marine organism deposits: oysters, corals, sea-urchin fossils; annual sediment rate ~0.1 mm
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Tectonic movement: Alpine orogeny uplifted the terrain to form today's slopes
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Jurassic Geological Evolution Timeline (200-Million-Year Epic)
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 🪨 The Science of Fossil Formation
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: Stage 1: organism dies and sinks to the seafloor; soft tissue decomposes
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: Stage 2: shell buried under sediment; carbonate shell preserved intact
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: Stage 3: continuous compaction; thickness increases ~10 cm per thousand years
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: Stage 4: chemical change; limestone and marl consolidate
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: Stage 5: crust uplift then erosion exposes fossils; minerals released
lessons.0.slides.4.points.5: Modern result: each kilogram of soil contains hundreds of micro-fossil fragments
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Kimmeridgian vs Portlandian
lessons.0.slides.5.content: The two most important soil types in Chablis both formed in the Late Jurassic: Kimmeridgian (~155 million years ago) and Portlandian (~150 million years ago). A mere 5-million-year difference yet they produce radically different soil composition and wine styles.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Kimmeridgian vs Portlandian
lessons.0.slides.7.title: 🔬 Geological Influences on Wine
lessons.0.slides.7.points.0: Fossil content: releases minerals, imparting savouriness and salinity
lessons.0.slides.7.points.1: Calcium carbonate: affects soil pH and drainage
lessons.0.slides.7.points.2: Clay ratio: affects water retention and wine body
lessons.0.slides.7.points.3: Trace elements: iron, magnesium, potassium — influence aromas and flavours
lessons.0.slides.7.points.4: Soil depth: determines root depth and hydric stress

lessons.1.title: Chablis' Kimmeridgian Miracle
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Chablis' Kimmeridgian Miracle
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 17 min
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Deep exploration of the secrets of Chablis' unique soil
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Kimmeridgian: The Soul of Chablis
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Kimmeridgian soil is a prerequisite for Chablis Grand Cru and Premier Cru. The soil takes its name from the village of Kimmeridge in Dorset, England, and the same geological layer extends into Chablis, France. A marl rich in small oyster fossils gives Chablis white wines their incomparable minerality, savouriness, and oyster-shell character.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🦪 Key Characteristics of Kimmeridgian
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: Small oyster fossils (Exogyra virgula): 2–3 cm, extremely abundant, thousands per cubic metre
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: Grey-green marl: rich in organic matter and minerals, CaCO₃ content 45–55%
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Layered structure: alternating limestone and clay, each layer 10–30 cm thick
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: High calcium carbonate: ~40–60%, pH 7.8–8.2, slightly alkaline
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Good drainage: prevents waterlogging at roots; infiltration rate ~10–15 cm/hour
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Cool soil temperature: 2–3 °C cooler than surroundings in summer — slows ripening, preserves acidity
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 📏 Chablis Soil Profile (0–150 cm depth)
lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: 0–20 cm: topsoil — dark brown, 2–3% organic matter, high root density
lessons.1.slides.3.points.1: 20–50 cm: main rooting zone — Kimmeridgian marl, grey-green, extremely fossil-rich
lessons.1.slides.3.points.2: 50–80 cm: subsoil — more limestone, drainage layer, penetrable by roots
lessons.1.slides.3.points.3: 80–120 cm: parent rock layer — hard limestone, roots enter along cracks
lessons.1.slides.3.points.5: Key: roots typically reach 100–150 cm, following cracks to seek water and nutrients
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Micro-Geological Differences Among the Seven Grand Crus
lessons.1.slides.5.title: The Seven Grand Crus: Location
lessons.1.slides.5.content: All seven Chablis Grand Crus sit on the same right-bank slope of the Serein river, all on Kimmeridgian soil. This south-southwest-facing slope provides ideal sun exposure and drainage — the position where Kimmeridgian soil reaches its greatest potential.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: ⭐ The Seven Chablis Grand Crus
lessons.1.slides.6.points.0: Blanchot (12.7 ha) — northernmost, most elegant and refined
lessons.1.slides.6.points.1: Les Clos (26 ha) — largest, most powerful
lessons.1.slides.6.points.5: Les Preuses (11.4 ha) — prominent floral character
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Grand Cru vs Petit Chablis
lessons.1.slides.8.title: Tasting the Influence of Kimmeridgian
lessons.1.slides.8.content: Kimmeridgian soil imparts Chablis' signature 'gunflint' character (goût de pierre à fusil), oyster-shell aromas, and unmatched minerality and savouriness. These traits are already apparent in youth and evolve with age into more complex iodine, flint, and wet-stone notes. This is a terroir code that no other Chardonnay region in the world can replicate.

lessons.2.title: Soil Differences: Côte de Nuits vs Côte de Beaune
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Soil Differences: Côte de Nuits vs Côte de Beaune
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 18 min
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Understanding the geological differences between red and white wine appellations
lessons.2.slides.1.title: One Ridge, Different Soils
lessons.2.slides.1.content: The Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune share the same north-south escarpment, but their soil compositions differ significantly. The Côte de Nuits is dominated by limestone mixed with clay — ideal for Pinot Noir; the northern (Corton-Charlemagne) and southern (Meursault-Puligny) sections of the Côte de Beaune are dominated by limestone — ideal for Chardonnay. These differences stem from different Jurassic depositional environments.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Côte de Nuits vs Côte de Beaune Soils
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🍇 Soil Characteristics by Village
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: Gevrey-Chambertin: clay mixed with gravel, iron-rich (Fe₂O₃ 10–15 ppm) — powerful wine body
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: Chambolle-Musigny: thin limestone (30–40 cm), excellent drainage — elegant and delicate
lessons.2.slides.3.points.2: Vosne-Romanée: perfect limestone-clay balance (55%/35%), warm microclimate
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: Meursault: white marl, reflects sunlight (albedo 15–20%) — rich whites
lessons.2.slides.3.points.4: Puligny-Montrachet: thin limestone (35–45 cm), excellent drainage — elegant minerality
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Pommard: deep red clay (60–80 cm), good water retention — full-bodied
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 🧪 Soil Chemical Composition Comparison Table (% by mass)
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: Côte de Nuits red clay: SiO₂ 45–50% | Al₂O₃ 12–15% | Fe₂O₃ 8–12% | CaCO₃ 15–25%
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: Côte de Beaune white marl: SiO₂ 25–35% | Al₂O₃ 5–8% | Fe₂O₃ 2–4% | CaCO₃ 50–65%
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: Kimmeridgian marl: SiO₂ 30–40% | Al₂O₃ 8–12% | Fe₂O₃ 3–6% | CaCO₃ 45–55%
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: Key difference: Côte de Nuits iron 3–4× higher; Côte de Beaune carbonate 2–3× higher
lessons.2.slides.4.points.4: pH: Côte de Nuits 7.0–7.5 | Côte de Beaune 7.5–8.2 | Chablis 7.8–8.3
lessons.2.slides.4.points.5: Organic matter: Côte de Nuits 2.5–3.5% | Côte de Beaune 1.5–2.5% | Chablis 1.8–2.8%
lessons.2.slides.5.title: The Influence of Iron
lessons.2.slides.5.content: The soils of many Côte de Nuits plots are rich in iron oxides, giving them their distinctive red-brown colour. Iron influences aromatic development in the grape — often contributing red-berry, rose, and even 'blood' characteristics. The soils of Clos de Tart, Romanée-Conti, and similar plots are notably iron-rich, which is one source of their complexity.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 💎 Le Montrachet's Perfect Soil
lessons.2.slides.6.points.0: Location: on the boundary of Puligny and Chassagne, mid-slope
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Soil depth: only 30–40 cm, underlain by hard limestone
lessons.2.slides.6.points.5: Result: world's greatest white wine — perfect minerality, depth, and ageing potential
lessons.2.slides.7.title: 🧠 Côte de Nuits vs Côte de Beaune Soil Quiz
lessons.3.title: Trace Elements and Flavor Expression
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Trace Elements and Flavor Expression
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 16 min
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Exploring how soil chemistry influences wine flavour
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Soil Is More Than a Support Medium
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Traditional thinking held that the minerals absorbed by the vine from the soil are too minuscule to affect flavour directly. But the latest research shows that trace elements in the soil — iron, manganese, zinc, copper, and others — however tiny in quantity, can significantly influence the vine's metabolism, enzyme activity, and the formation of flavour precursors. This explains why the same variety produces radically different flavours in different soils.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🔬 Influence of Key Trace Elements
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Iron (Fe): influences pigment formation; imparts 'blood', minerality — ideal concentration 8–12 ppm
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Manganese (Mn): participates in photosynthesis; influences aroma precursors — ideal 25–50 ppm
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Zinc (Zn): influences enzyme activity; promotes aromatic development — ideal 15–30 ppm
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Copper (Cu): antioxidant role; influences ageing potential — ideal 5–10 ppm
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: Magnesium (Mg): core of chlorophyll; affects photosynthesis efficiency — ideal 150–300 ppm
lessons.3.slides.2.points.5: Potassium (K): influences sugar accumulation and acid balance — ideal 200–400 ppm
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 🦠 Soil Microbiome Ecosystem
lessons.3.slides.3.points.0: Bacteria: 100 million–1 billion per gram of soil; decompose organic matter and release nutrients
lessons.3.slides.3.points.1: Fungi: 100,000–1 million per gram; form mycorrhizal networks to aid absorption
lessons.3.slides.3.points.2: Actinobacteria: produce growth hormones and antibiotics; promote plant health
lessons.3.slides.3.points.3: Protozoa: 1,000–10,000 per gram; control pathogenic bacteria
lessons.3.slides.3.points.4: Earthworms: 100–500 per m²; improve soil structure
lessons.3.slides.3.points.5: Biodynamic advantage: enhances microbial diversity and activity, strengthening terroir expression
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Conventional Farming vs Biodynamic Soil Microbial Activity
lessons.3.slides.5.title: The Critical Role of Calcium Carbonate
lessons.3.slides.5.content: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) in limestone is one of the most important components of Burgundy soils. High CaCO₃ provides excellent drainage, regulates soil pH in the ideal range (7.5–8.5), and promotes microbial activity. Research shows soils with 50–70% CaCO₃ produce the most elegant, refined wines.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: ⚗️ The Effect of Soil pH
lessons.3.slides.6.points.0: pH 7–7.5 (slightly alkaline): most ideal; common in Meursault and Puligny
lessons.3.slides.6.points.1: pH 7.5–8 (alkaline): high limestone content; elegant minerality
lessons.3.slides.6.points.2: pH 6.5–7 (neutral): more clay; fuller wine body
lessons.3.slides.6.points.3: pH effects: nutrient availability, microbial activity, root development
lessons.3.slides.6.points.4: Burgundy advantage: alkaline soils maintain high acidity, balancing the wine
lessons.3.slides.7.title: Limestone vs Clay Chemical Differences
lessons.3.slides.8.title: Clay vs Limestone Flavour Matrix
lessons.3.slides.9.title: The Role of Soil Microorganisms
lessons.3.slides.9.content: Soil is not dead mineral matter but a living ecosystem. Each gram of soil contains billions of microorganisms — bacteria, fungi, yeasts — that decompose organic matter, release nutrients, produce growth hormones, and even influence flavour precursors in the grape. Biodynamics (Biodynamie) particularly emphasises soil microbial activity — the core philosophy of top estates like Leroy and DRC.

lessons.4.title: Soil Analysis and Parcel Selection
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Soil Analysis and Parcel Selection
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 16 min
lessons.4.slides.0.description: Learn how to assess soil quality and parcel potential
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Professional Soil Analysis Methods
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Modern vineyard management requires scientific soil analysis. Professional analysis covers: physical properties (texture, structure, depth), chemical properties (pH, organic matter, minerals), and biological properties (microbial population, activity). Top estates typically conduct a full soil analysis every 5 years and basic monitoring annually.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🔍 Key Indicators in Soil Assessment
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: Texture: ratio of sand, silt, clay (ideal: sandy loam ~40–60 / 20–30 / 20–30%)
lessons.4.slides.2.points.1: Depth: topsoil depth (ideal: 40–80 cm — not too shallow, not too deep)
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: Drainage: infiltration rate (ideal: moderately fast, 10–20 cm/hour)
lessons.4.slides.2.points.3: Organic matter: 1–3% is ideal; too high can impair drainage
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: pH: 7–8 ideal (slightly alkaline); too acid or too alkaline is detrimental
lessons.4.slides.2.points.5: Calcium carbonate: 50–70% optimal — provides minerality and drainage
lessons.4.slides.2.points.6: NPK: moderate levels (N <2%, P 20–40 ppm, K 200–400 ppm); too high is harmful to quality
lessons.4.slides.3.title: 🎯 Parcel Potential Scoring System (100 points)
lessons.4.slides.3.points.0: Soil composition (30 pts) — limestone ratio, clay ratio, organic matter, pH
lessons.4.slides.3.points.1: Topographic position (25 pts) — aspect, gradient, altitude, upper/mid/lower slope
lessons.4.slides.3.points.2: Drainage (15 pts) — infiltration rate, soil depth, water table
lessons.4.slides.3.points.3: Microclimate (15 pts) — frost risk, sunshine hours, wind protection, diurnal range
lessons.4.slides.3.points.4: Historical performance (10 pts) — past vintage quality, producer reputation, market recognition
lessons.4.slides.3.points.5: Surrounding environment (5 pts) — forest shelter, water source, stone walls, neighbouring parcel quality
lessons.4.slides.3.points.6: 90+: Grand Cru potential | 75–90: Premier Cru potential | 60–75: Village | <60: Regional
lessons.4.slides.4.title: How to Identify a High-Potential Parcel?
lessons.4.slides.4.content: Identifying high-potential parcels requires integrating soil, topography, and climate. Burgundy's traditional wisdom says the best parcels are typically on mid-slope, south-east facing, limestone-dominated soils, with moderate soil depth (not too deep, not too shallow). But there are exceptions: Romanée-Conti sits on a relatively gentle gradient, yet excels through a unique soil composition.
lessons.4.slides.5.title: ⭐ Shared Characteristics of Top Parcels
lessons.4.slides.5.points.1: Moderate soil depth (40–60 cm) with rock below
lessons.4.slides.5.points.3: East or south-east facing; no western exposure
lessons.4.slides.5.points.6: Forest or stone-wall microclimate shelter nearby
lessons.4.slides.6.title: Upper Slope vs Mid-Slope vs Lower Slope
lessons.4.slides.7.title: Parcel Re-Evaluation Under Climate Change
lessons.4.slides.7.content: As the climate warms, once-desirable warm parcels now risk over-ripening, while cooler, higher-altitude or north-facing plots are being reconsidered. Some producers are experimenting with parcels previously considered too cool. Within the next 10–20 years, Burgundy's definition of 'ideal parcel' may be rewritten.
lessons.4.slides.8.title: 💡 Practical Tips
lessons.4.slides.8.points.0: When visiting a vineyard, observe soil colour (red-brown vs white)
lessons.4.slides.8.points.1: Note gradient and aspect (confirm with a compass)
lessons.4.slides.8.points.2: Observe surrounding vegetation (certain plants indicate soil type)
lessons.4.slides.8.points.3: Taste wines from different parcels of the same vintage side by side
lessons.4.slides.8.points.4: Read geological maps (BRGM — the French Geological Survey — provides these)
lessons.4.slides.8.points.5: Join a guided specialist tour to deepen your terroir understanding
